title: How to Earn and Spend Shop Rewards Points in the Gerald App
summary: Learn how to earn, view, and redeem shop rewards points in the Gerald app with practical tips to maximize every coin and stretch your everyday budget.
body_markdown:
Join Gerald for a new way to manage your finances.


Cash advances with no fees.


[Get Started](https://joingerald.com/#signup)


You open Gerald while checking whether your next paycheck will cover the basics, and a coin balance catches your eye. The obvious question is simple: **can those shop rewards points reduce what you pay, or are they just another app decoration?**


They can help, but only if you treat them like a small spending offset rather than a savings account. Gerald coins come from everyday in-app actions, mobile plan activity, and eligible BNPL behavior, then convert into rewards for purchases inside Cornerstore. They aren't cash advances, cash-back dollars, or credit. They're account-linked store value, so the practical move is to earn consistently, check the balance, and redeem before the value becomes difficult to use.

## What Shop Rewards Points Mean Inside Gerald


Gerald's shop rewards points are best understood as **coins held inside your Gerald account** . You can earn them through activities such as playing games, completing surveys, finishing partner tasks, paying mobile plans, and using eligible BNPL features. The balance stays connected to your account, so you don't need to track separate coupons, paper receipts, or a loose collection of promo codes.


The important limitation is where you can spend them. Gerald coins are designed for redemption inside **Gerald's Cornerstore** , where they can help offset purchases of household essentials and other available items. They aren't a general-purpose payment method, and you shouldn't count them as money you can transfer to your bank account or use at an unrelated retailer. For a broader explanation of Gerald's connected advance, store, mobile, and repayment experience, see[how Gerald works](https://joingerald.com/how-it-works) .


### Coins are useful only when you use them


A points balance feels rewarding, but the balance itself doesn't pay a bill. The value appears when you apply coins to an eligible Cornerstore purchase and see the amount due fall. That makes the timing of redemption more important than building an impressive-looking total.


Large rewards programs show why this matters. Americans earned about **$47 billion in credit card rewards in 2024** and redeemed about **$43 billion** , while a separate industry estimate placed the global value of unredeemed loyalty points at **$50 billion** . Those figures cover broader rewards ecosystems, not Gerald specifically, but they illustrate the central issue with points: issuance creates potential value, while redemption determines whether consumers receive it. The figures are reported in[credit card rewards statistics from The Motley Fool](https://www.fool.com/money/research/credit-card-rewards-statistics/) .


**Practical rule:** Treat coins as a discount waiting to be used, not as cash waiting to grow.


If you're comparing Gerald with other loyalty tools, a guide to designing a[profit-driven points program](https://npoint.digital/loyalty-points-system/) can help explain why merchants use points to encourage repeat purchases. For your purposes, keep the rule simpler: earn from actions you'd complete anyway, then spend the balance on an essential you already planned to buy.


## Ways to Earn Coins and Rewards


Gerald gives you several routes to build a coin balance, but they don't all deserve equal attention. Start with actions that fit into your existing routine, then skip anything that demands too much time, personal information, or spending for a reward that doesn't justify the effort.


### Play-to-earn games


Mini-games can award coins for reaching milestones or maintaining daily streaks. The best approach is to check the terms before starting, note the required action, and stop once the reward no longer justifies your time. Gerald's[Play to Earn feature](https://joingerald.com/play-to-earn) is most useful as a short daily habit, not an excuse to spend long sessions chasing tiny increments.


### Surveys and partner tasks


Surveys and sponsored offers can add coins after you submit the required information or complete a qualifying action. Some offers may require verification, and some may remain pending until a partner confirms completion. Read the instructions carefully, especially if an offer has a cooldown timer, purchase condition, or identity check.


Paid tasks can include simple digital chores or partner activities. Don't assume every listed task is worth doing. Compare the time, data requested, and redemption requirement before you commit.


### Mobile and BNPL activity


Active mobile plan use may trigger periodic coin drops connected to your line or plan activity. BNPL rewards should be treated differently from approval. Coins are tied to **completed installments or qualifying usage** , not receiving approval for a purchase. Use BNPL for an essential you already need, and never create a purchase just to earn points.


Referral bonuses and seasonal promotions may increase your balance when Gerald makes them available. Their terms can change, so check the offer window and completion requirements instead of relying on an old promotion.


For shoppers trying to stretch household spending, a[cashback grocery strategy for debt](https://usetoya.com/blog/cashback-at-grocery-stores/) offers a useful general principle: rewards work best when they attach to planned necessities rather than impulse purchases. Apply the same discipline here.


## Where to View Your Points Balance


Start on Gerald's **home tab** . Look for the balance widget that displays your current coin total and recent reward activity. This first number is useful, but don't stop there. A headline balance may not tell you whether every coin has cleared or whether older rewards carry a use-by condition.


### Read the balance in layers


Tap into the rewards or wallet area to inspect the activity history. Look for these distinctions:


- **Current balance:** Coins available to apply now.
- **Pending coins:** Rewards still waiting for a task, transaction, or partner offer to clear.
- **Lifetime earnings:** The total you've earned over time, which may be higher than your spendable total.
- **Expiration details:** Any date or condition attached to older coins.
- **Redemption preview:** The estimated buying power shown before you reach checkout.


The difference between lifetime earned and currently usable coins matters. A task can appear in your history without immediately increasing the amount available for a purchase, especially when a partner needs to verify completion. If your balance looks lower than expected, check the transaction status before repeating the task.


### Make the check part of your routine


Review recent activity after completing a survey, game milestone, mobile action, or installment. That quick check confirms whether Gerald recorded the event and helps you catch a missing requirement while the details are still fresh.


Don't confuse the coin widget with your cash-advance eligibility or BNPL amount. Coins are store rewards. They don't increase the amount of cash you can transfer, and they don't remove repayment obligations on an advance or installment.


## How to Redeem Shop Rewards Points at Checkout


Use coins when you're buying something you need from Cornerstore, not when you're browsing for a reason to spend. Add the item to your cart, review the subtotal, and continue to checkout. Before selecting the BNPL option, look for the **coins payment toggle** or rewards control.


If your balance covers only part of the cart, apply a partial amount rather than waiting for a larger balance. A slider or input field may let you choose how many coins to use. Watch the total after applying them. The checkout should show a separate discount or rewards line that reduces the amount remaining.


### Check the payment combination


Coins may be used alongside one BNPL installment, but they aren't designed to combine with multiple split payments. If you select several payment splits, the rewards control may be unavailable or the order may require a different payment arrangement.


Minimum redemption thresholds also matter. If the balance falls below the applicable minimum, the app may block redemption even though the coins remain visible. That isn't a reason to buy something unnecessary. Keep the balance for the next planned Cornerstore purchase, and check the terms before assuming every coin can be applied to every cart.


**Before tapping submit:** Confirm the coin amount, the remaining installment total, and the final payment schedule.


Cancellation and refunds deserve attention. If you cancel an order after applying coins, the system may return eligible coins to your rewards balance rather than sending them to your bank. A refund can also take time to appear, particularly if the order or payment is still processing. Check the transaction history instead of assuming the coins disappeared permanently.


The checkout screen is where the value becomes real. If coins reduce the price of a household staple you needed anyway, the redemption is doing its job. If you're changing your shopping plan just to use them, the discount may be less meaningful than it looks.


## Getting Real Value From Every Coin


My strongest recommendation is simple: **redeem smaller balances when they can offset an essential purchase** . Hoarding sounds financially responsible, but it creates two risks. You delay a benefit you could use today, and you give expiration rules or inactivity a chance to erase the value.


A practical benchmark for points-based rewards is **3% to 10% back per dollar spent** , with the first reward structured after **1 to 3 purchases** , according to[Smile.io's points reward guidance](https://blog.smile.io/how-many-points-should-your-first-reward-be-valued-at/) . That benchmark isn't a promise about Gerald's specific conversion rate. Use it as a way to judge whether a redemption feels meaningful relative to the purchase and the effort required to earn the coins.
